content:
Hi!

I'm working on a framework to help specify multi-tape Turing machines over at my cslib fork (NB: the following text reflects my current ideas, which is a bit ahead of the code in the repository). Some of you might have seen my talk at leaning in 2026. I would like to share my progress since (and until) then and potentially start a discussion about if this is going in the right direction and if this is eventually desired for cslib or not.

The idea is to build a compositional framework for constructing Turing machines. As an example, the core of a SAT verifier in this language would be as follows (the numbers specify the tape indices to operate on: 0 contains the formula, 1 the assignment as a list of all positive variables and 2 is an auxiliary tape):

all_list 0 2 (any_list 0 2 (case_literal 0
    (contains 1 0 2)
    (contains 1 0 2;ₜ negateBool 2)
))

My hope is that both verification of semantics and resource consumption should be relatively simple in this framework.

In the end, each TM constructed this way is an actual machine working on tapes with symbols, i.e. it's not a different machine definition which is important if we want to talk about resource bounds. Furthermore, all machines are constructed from a set of base machines like move_right i (move the head on tape i one cell to the right), write i c (write symbol c to the current head position at tape i), while_eq i c tm (run TM tm as long as the symbol read on tape i equals c) and sequential composition (written ;ₜ above). Note that all machines here do not necessarily compute functions, but instead start with an arbitrary initial tape configuration and (if they halt) conclude in a new tape configuration.

The abstraction for it to be able to work on lists (actually almost any lean type as we will see later) is achieved by the encoding: The work alphabet is just (, ) and the contents of each tape is guaranteed to be a properly parenthesized string before and after execution of a TM, unless it is a low-level machine. This allows us to talk about tapes being encodings of inductive Data where | ls : List Data → Data. Furthermore, the position of the tape head can be specified by a List ℕ (the longest chain of indices into the lists leading to the head) plus an indicator if it is positioned on the opening or closing parenthesis. This means that there is a way to talk about the semantics of TMs not on tapes but on a type similar to Data × (List ℕ) × Bool (plus a proof that the List ℕ is valid for the Data).

Being able to talk about situations where the tape head is inside such a structure is important for sub-linear space machines which need a way to navigate through a long read-only tape. As long as the nesting depth is bounded by a constant, a TM can freely navigate inside such a data structure in constant space (although it can only loop through lists or move to an element indexed by a constant because it cannot count finite amounts). As soon as it has logarithmic space, it can also navigate to any index.

We can encode numbers in binary by encoding the bits 0 as ((())) and 1 as (()()). Since the bits have the same encoding length, it means that we can update numbers (as members of Fin 2^n) in-place.

Talking about encoding: By defining an injective encoding into Data, we can also define how such a machine operates on almost any lean type. This is what I did with the SAT verifier example above:

public abbrev Var := ℕ
public inductive Literal where
  | pos (v : Var)
  | neg (v : Var)

public instance : DataEnc Literal where
  toData
    -- re-use the already defined encoding for tuples and Nat
    | Literal.pos v => DataEnc.toData (0, v)
    | Literal.neg v => DataEnc.toData (1, v)
  ...

At some point, this can of course be automatic for any non-recursive inductive data structure and it could also create a suitable match combinator for the data type.

If an Assignment is a List Var that contains the positive variables, then the desired semantics of evaluating a literal under an assignment is

public def evalLiteral (a : Assignments) : Literal → Bool
  | Literal.pos v => a.contains v
  | Literal.neg v => !(a.contains v)

And now if we extract the sub-routine for evaluating literals from the full sat verifier machine above as

def satVerifyEvalLiteral : MultiTapeTM 5 Char :=
  case_literal 0
    (contains 1 0 2)
    (contains 1 0 2;ₜ negateBool 2)

we can state its semantics as

lemma satVerifyEvalLiteral.computes_fun :
  computes_function_read_read_push
    satVerifyEvalLiteral
    (fun lit ass => evalLiteral ass lit)
    0 1 2 := by
  let h_pos := computes_function_read_read_push_swap
    (contains.computes_fun (α := Var) (k := 5) (i := 1) (j := 0) (result := 2) (by decide))
  let h_neg := computes_function_seq₂ h_pos negateBool.computes_head_update
  exact case_literal.computes_fun (β := Assignments) (γ := Bool) _ _ (by decide) h_pos h_neg

I think the proof is longer than desired (simp; grind) because of the encoding type classes, but I'm still investigating that. Note that we did not need to handle the case where we have an invalid encoding (for example the constructor index for Literal could be greater than 1) because computes_function_read_read_push, when applied to fun (lit : Literal) (ass : List Var), has the precondition that the currently pointed-to element at tape 0 is a valid encoding of Literal and that tape 1 contains a valid encoding of List Var). If you then use satVerifyEvalLiteral inside any_list applied to List Literal, the preconditions nicely translate to/from the outside.

In summary, I think this is a framework that allows to conveniently build complex TMs (I'm currently working on a universal TM) without the need to juggle states (in fact explicitly specifying state transition functions is only needed for the elementary machines read, right, ...) and instead work with loops, lists etc. and it allows to talk about the behavior of TMs in a type-safe manner.

Some areas where help would be appreciated is a way to specify general functions on multi-tape TMs: For example you see that I use computes_function_read_read_push, which means that we have a function that reads inputs from two tapes and pushes its output to a third tape which is expected to be a list and the tape head is at the very beginning of it (in order to prepend something without overwriting other data). I'm a bit struggling to generalize this to an arbitrary number of inputs, outputs and updates that optimally also works with simp.

And then of course there is the work of specifying all the intermediate-level machines and specifying their semantics nicely in simp lemmas.

Looking forward to all your comments!

Christian
One thing we have learnt with the Prog framework is that specifying single step transitions is tedious. We can now program Turing machines using lean code directly.

I know it is tedious, but I fear there is no way around building the foundations using single-step transitions. I don't see how you would translate lean code to space-efficient Turing machines without going through such a framework that specifies exactly which data is read-only and which data is appended or inserted where. How would your translation of the following code look like:

public def evalFormula (a : Assignments) (f : Formula) : Bool :=
  f.all fun c => c.any (fun l => match l with
    | Literal.pos v => a.contains v
    | Literal.neg v => !(a.contains v))

Or what do you mean by "program Turing machines using lean code directly"?
We can specify per step transitions. We just specify them inside a prog.
As you can see in the Algolean code for single tape TMs we specify the actions of transition functions through queries
Extending it to multitape machines is trivial
In the multitape version you just specify the tape id as an extra parameter to each query. You only allow operations on valid tapes

@Shreyas Srinivas as we have discussed at some length, there are good reasons we may not want to use a monadic/query framework for every single piece of formalization in CSLib. I do not think it is productive to rehash this conversation in every single thread.

@chris477 I had left some initial comments on cslib#384, but had not taken too deep a look, sorry for letting this slip through! Maybe this has diverged enough that it is worth making a new PR once your fork has caught up to this discussion? I am travelling so don't think I can have a look until at soonest the next week or so.
We are discussing TM models here. I am not even bringing up CSLib

I am merely pointing out that the difficulty in TMs arises from definitions where people first specify single step transition functions and then interpret them on tapes. In reality most complexity theory textbooks just describe TM operations like a program I.e. as acomplete multi step transition function.
This is the CSLib channel, and the discussion here is about Turing Machines in CSLib.

Chris Henson schrieb:

chris477 I had left some initial comments on cslib#384, but had not taken too deep a look, sorry for letting this slip through! Maybe this has diverged enough that it is worth making a new PR once your fork has caught up to this discussion? I am travelling so don't think I can have a look until at soonest the next week or so.

No worries! It's actually rather independent due to the fact that I just use right, write, etc. as elementary machines which I then combine, so it's only loosely coupled to the actual TM definition. I was even considering at some point to make this fully independent using type classes, but I don't think it's a good idea.

Chris Henson said:

This is the CSLib channel, and the discussion here is about Turing Machines in CSLib.

I appreciate that but we are discussing designs here, and a comparative discussion fits. I have already had a chat with Chris about integrating these two ideas a few weeks ago. I am mainly sharing my insight that specifying single steps matters (we also do that), but it gets easier to specify multi step transitions (which would include single step operations). It makes compositions simpler. The monadic nature of my framework or its adoption is orthogonal . It’s just a convenient concrete example to illustrate the point and show other ways of achieving compositionality.

@Chris Henson it would be great if you could have another look at my pr. I just opened a second (unrelated) pr that is just about tapes: it allows to view them as function on the integers instead of two lists, which is often better when many moves and writes are involved. Unrelated to that, I think that the current definition of space used (also already for single tapes) is inaccurate. I will probably submit another pr on that topic soon.

I just saw this PR. I think the view of bitapes as integer indexed cells makes it easier to define space complexity. I recommend getting it ready and merged asap. As for space complexity, I think multitape TMs are the cleanest model for expressing them, so I hope your PRs get merged soon.
@chris477 I left a review on cslib#499. Thanks for letting me know that your previous PR is ready to review, I'll have another look soon.
